safetyNote: Poisonous. Omphalotus olearius can cause severe nausea, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea, with a risk of dehydration. It is sometimes collected by mistake for chanterelles. If ingestion is suspected, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly and keep a sample for identification.

sections.title: Cap and true gills
sections.text: The smooth to slightly fibrillose cap is bright orange to coppery or orange-brown, often darker at the centre. It begins convex with an inrolled edge, then flattens or develops a central depression and a wavy margin; reported cap widths span roughly 6–20 cm. Its underside has numerous thin, sharp-edged, crowded orange true gills that run a long way down the stem. Some gills may fork near the cap edge, so a complete absence of forks is not a reliable test.

sections.title: Stem, flesh and growth
sections.text: The firm orange stem is sometimes off-centre, usually tapers toward the base and may darken there. Orange flesh continues through the cap and stem. Fruit bodies commonly form dense tufts whose stems converge on decaying hardwood, buried roots or a stump, especially olive or oak; a buried root can make a tuft seem to grow from bare soil. There is no ring or volva.

sections.title: Season, spores and light
sections.text: A wood-decaying fungus of southern and central Europe, especially Mediterranean areas, it fruits mainly from late summer through autumn and sometimes into winter in mild climates. Its spore deposit is cream-white; the smooth microscopic spores are broadly rounded to ellipsoid. Fresh gills can give a faint greenish glow in complete darkness, but this is variable and must not be used to identify a specimen.

sections.title: Confusion with chanterelles
sections.text: Chanterelles such as Cantharellus cibarius have blunt, thick, often branching ridges fused to the cap flesh, not separable blade-like gills. They normally fruit from soil in association with living trees rather than as a tuft from decaying wood. The false chanterelle, Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca, also has much more extensively forked gills. Use several characters together; a colour match or the presence or absence of glow alone is unsafe.

traits: Orange to coppery cap, convex at first then depressed or funnel-like with a wavy edge
Thin crowded true orange gills running well down the stem; occasional forks may occur
Usually dense clusters on decaying wood, stumps or buried broadleaf roots
Orange flesh through the cap and stem; stem tapers and darkens near the base
Cream-white spore deposit; faint gill glow is variable and not diagnostic
Mainly southern and central Europe, particularly Mediterranean woodland
